summary: 3GPP introduced network slicing for mobile networks. This informational document describes how to realize 5G network slices in the transport network using current IP and MPLS technologies.

eli5.summary: One road can be shared as separate lanes for different kinds of vehicles. This explains how to carve a network into such lanes for 5G.

subtitle: How to build isolated network lanes for 5G services using standard IP and MPLS.

tldr.problem: 5G networks need to slice traffic into isolated logical partitions with guaranteed quality, but the transport network uses standard IP and MPLS technologies that were not designed with slicing in mind.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes how to create RFC 9543 Network Slices by mapping 5G service requirements to transport layer VPNs, QoS classes, and edge resource controls, using existing L2VPN and L3VPN services with fine-grained admission control at the provider edge and coarse-grained QoS in the core.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now realize 5G slices without new protocols, leveraging proven IP/MPLS techniques to isolate traffic, enforce bandwidth contracts, and meet service level objectives across provider networks.

today: RFC 9889 is Informational and describes pragmatic approaches that are already deployed in mobile networks. It does not define new standards but provides guidance on how to combine existing RFCs (notably RFC 9543, RFC 4364, RFC 4664) to realize 5G network slicing in production networks using IP and MPLS.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
5G networks require network slicing, a way to partition a shared network into separate logical networks, each with its own performance guarantees and isolation. This is not new to networking—it is similar to what IP VPNs do for dedicated customer networks.

The novelty in 5G is that the Radio Access Network (RAN), Core Network (CN), and Transport Network (TN) must all support slicing together. This RFC focuses on the Transport Network part: how to realize 5G Network Slices as defined in RFC 9543 using existing IP and MPLS technologies rather than inventing new protocols.

The document assumes that customer sites (where 5G functions run) are overprovisioned with short distances, so basic QoS logic is sufficient inside them. The provider network carries the slice services between customer sites, using standard L2VPN and L3VPN service instances for separation, fine-grained resource control at the network edge, and coarse-grained sharing of transit resources.
sections.eli5: The RFC explains how a phone network can split itself into separate slices—one for video, one for smart devices, one for emergency services—without needing to redesign the underlying network hardware.

sections.title: Architecture and Orchestration
sections.content:
The RFC defines three orchestration domains: the customer site, the provider network, and the 3GPP domains (RAN and CN). An Attachment Circuit (AC) is the logical connection between a Customer Edge (CE) device and a Provider Edge (PE) device; it marks the boundary between what the customer manages and what the provider manages.

The document introduces the concepts of distributed CE and distributed PE—logical functions that may span multiple physical devices. This flexibility allows diverse deployment models, from simple point-to-point links to complex cloud environments.

A key innovation is that the RFC defines Transport Network Slices as a separate concept from 5G Network Slices. A single 5G slice may map to one or more Transport Network Slices (1-to-N), multiple 5G slices may share one Transport Network Slice (M-to-1), or they may have a mixed mapping (M-to-N). The orchestration between the customer and provider domains is automated via standard YANG data models such as the Network Slice Service Model (NSSM) or Attachment Circuits as a Service (ACaaS).
sections.eli5: Different teams manage different parts of the network: the customer runs their 5G functions, the provider runs the network pipes, and they use a standard checklist to agree on who is responsible for what.

sections.title: Slice Handoff Methods
sections.content:
5G control plane uses 32-bit identifiers called S-NSSAIs to name slices, but these identifiers are not visible to the transport network. The RFC describes three handoff methods to map 5G slices to transport-visible identifiers:

VLAN Handoff: Each slice is assigned a VLAN ID. VLANs are local to the Attachment Circuit and represent logical interfaces. This is simple but requires mapping tables at each SDP and coordination between orchestrators for every new slice.

IP Handoff: S-NSSAIs are mapped to IP addresses, DSCP values, SRv6 locators, or IP subnets. A novel approach uses IPv6 address encoding to embed the S-NSSAI directly into 32 bits of the 128-bit IPv6 address, eliminating the need for mapping tables. However, changing S-NSSAI values requires changing IP addresses, which affects all hosts in the slice.

MPLS Label Handoff: The RFC describes three options (A, B, C) from RFC 4364 for interconnecting MPLS services over domain boundaries. Option B uses dynamically allocated MPLS labels with BGP communities to track which label belongs to which slice. Option C uses two-level label stacking (service labels and labeled unicast labels) to reduce forwarding table pressure on PEs when there are many slices.
sections.eli5: When traffic leaves the customer site and enters the network, someone needs to label it to say which slice it belongs to. The RFC shows three ways to do this: with VLAN stickers, with IP addresses, or with MPLS label stamps.

sections.title: QoS Mapping: 5G to Transport
sections.content:
The RFC defines two layers of Quality of Service. The 5G QoS Layer uses 5QI (5G QoS Indicator) values to specify per-traffic-class treatment in the RAN—things like scheduling weights and queue depths. The Transport Network QoS Layer uses at most 8 traffic classes on transit links to keep routers manageable.

Since 5G functions can set DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) to encode the 5QI, the provider network can see it at the Service Demarcation Point. The RFC describes two models:

5QI-Unaware Model: All flows in a slice get the same transport QoS treatment regardless of their 5QI, mapped to a single transport QoS class. This is simpler to operate when there are many slices.

5QI-Aware Model: Each 5QI maps to its own transport QoS class, giving finer control but requiring more classes. This uses MPLS Traffic Class (3 bits, 8 values) or DSCP (6 bits, 64 values).

At the PE, inbound edge resource control enforces per-slice bandwidth limits via policing and rate limiting. Outbound edge resource control uses hierarchical schedulers and shapers to guarantee rates per slice and per QoS class. Transit routers see only the outer header's QoS marking and apply coarse-grained per-hop behavior, which naturally isolates slices with minimal state.
sections.eli5: The network has two layers of quality control: inside the 5G network, different apps get different treatment; on the transport network, all packets from one slice follow the same rules, and the network edge makes sure no one slice hogs all the bandwidth.

sections.title: Provider Edge Underlay Transport
sections.content:
The RFC defines two models for how PEs handle traffic within the constraints of a Network Resource Partition (NRP):

5QI-Unaware PE Model: The PE does not distinguish 5QI values. It applies the same resource allocation to all traffic in the slice, ignoring internal QoS markings. This is operationally simpler and suitable for deployments with many slices where per-5QI treatment is not required.

5QI-Aware PE Model: The PE recognizes DSCP-encoded 5QI and allocates buffer and scheduling resources per 5QI within the slice. This provides granular control but requires more PE resources and is typically used in networks with fewer slices or where per-QoS guarantees are critical.

Both models share the same overall philosophy: fine-grained control at the edges (customer attachment points) and coarse-grained sharing in the middle (provider backbone). This balance minimizes state in the core while meeting service level objectives at the edges.
sections.eli5: The network edge is strict about enforcement—each slice gets exactly what it paid for—but the middle of the network is relaxed, allowing slices to share lanes when they're not using their full allotment.

sections.title: Capacity Planning and Management
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that network slicing cannot succeed without proper capacity planning. The slicing model is based on the assumption that the provider network is dimensioned so that slices do not cause congestion even when using coarse-grained transit QoS.

The document briefly covers bandwidth characterization using Committed Information Rate (CIR) and Peak Information Rate (PIR), and mentions Traffic Engineering (TE) techniques—including equal-cost load balancing, segment routing, and bandwidth reservations—to distribute traffic evenly and avoid bottlenecks.

For managed CE services (where the provider operates the customer edge), edge admission control can be shared between the CE and PE. For scalability in very large deployments, the RFC notes that single Network Resource Partitions simplify the model, and multiple NRPs are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Even with the best isolation, if the network is too full, slices will suffer. The RFC explains that operators must plan capacity carefully, using traffic engineering tools to keep lanes from getting too crowded.
